steps.title: A normal Tuesday morning
steps.say: An invented 32-bed emergency department with two CT scanners and 122 ward beds behind it, at 07:00 on a Tuesday after sixteen weeks of history: about 140 arrivals a day, a fifth admitted. Models fitted on that history and tested on the last two weeks: an arrival profile by hour and weekday, an admission classifier, a length-of-stay model (which turns out no better than the median by triage level, and says so) and the wards' turnover. Encounters carry a hashed token and an age band, nothing else about the person.

steps.title: The next 24 hours as the models see them
steps.say: Expected arrivals per hour with an 80% band and the share at triage 1-2; ward discharges and admissions expected hour by hour and the free beds that leaves; and the baseline simulation: the department run forward twelve hours thirty times from its live state, with bands on waiting, boarding, the CT queue and the KPIs.

steps.title: Four hours pass: a surge and a discharge slowdown
steps.say: The clock moves to 11:00. The generator is told what happens, which is the demo's way of injecting a disruption: thirty injured patients arrive over an hour from 10:00, and the wards process discharges at 40% of their normal rate for eight hours from 09:00. The service sees only the encounters and events.

steps.title: Three more are announced by FHIR, and the board goes red
steps.say: The ambulance service sends a FHIR Bundle: three Encounter resources with a triage level, an age and a reason, two of them valid and one without a timezone, which is refused. The accepted arrivals join the live state. The capacity view now carries alerts: the waiting room, the nurse ratio, the CT queue and the ward.

steps.title: Predicted boarding and waiting, with and without action
steps.say: The simulation again, from the new state, told what bed management knows: discharges are slow for six more hours. Baseline against a package of actions a charge nurse might take: six surge beds, two extra nurses on the day and evening shifts, and a discharge push on the wards. Peak waiting, boarding and door-to-bed with bands, side by side. The honest finding: the actions help, and the surge still takes most of the day to clear, because the binding constraint is bed-hours.

steps.title: A staffing recommendation, proposed
steps.say: The optimiser: the P80 census per shift from the baseline runs, the nurses needed at a ratio of four, and the cheapest call-ins from the on-call pool by CP-SAT; surge beds and a discharge push added where the runs say they help. It is a proposal with a rationale and an expected effect. Nothing changes in the department.

steps.title: A person decides
steps.say: The charge nurse who proposed it cannot approve it; a viewer cannot either. The operations director approves, the call-ins become real shifts, and the capacity view shows the actions as active. Then the recommendation list and the audit log.
